Thoracic Skeleton

Sternum


   The sternum is divided into 3 main parts, the manubrium,
   body, and xiphoid process.

Manubrium:
Superior part of sternum
Site of articulation for the clavicles and costal cartilage of ribs 1 & 2

Body:
    Site of articulation for costal cartilage of ribs 2 to 7
   Contains the sternal angle also known as angle of Louis which
    is formed by the junction of manubrium and body of sternum.
    This angle can be palpated on your body as an inward
   projection below jugular notch.

Importance:
      It marks the attachment of the 2nd costal cartilage
     lies at T4/T5
     is a reference point when counting ribs and intercostal spaces
    level of bifurcation of trachea

Xiphoid Process:
    inferior part of sternum which is made up of a thin plate of
   hyaline cartilage which ossifies in adult life
    Site of articulation for costal cartilage of ribs 7 & 8

Classification of Ribs

1. According to features

TYPICAL RIBS: ribs 3 to 9
 -have similar anatomical features
  -All consist of a head, neck, body, and tubercle

ATYPICAL RIBS: 1st, 2nd, 10th, 11th, and 12th ribs
-have distinctive features

2. According to relation with sternum

TRUE RIBS: ribs 1 to 7
 -articulate with sternum anteriorly

FALSE RIBS: ribs 8 to 10
 - do not articulate with sternum anteriorly; their costal cartilages
join with  cartilage of the rib above

FLOATING RIBS: ribs 11 and 12
 -do not articulate with the sternum

3. According to articulation

VERTEBRO STERNAL RIBS: ribs 1 to 7
  -articulate with sternum anteriorly and vertebra posteriorly

VERTEBRO CHONDRAL RIBS: ribs 8 to 10
 -articulate with vertebra posteriorly and their costal cartilages
join with cartilage of the superior rib

VERTEBRAL RIBS (floating ribs): ribs 11 & 12
 -articulate with vertebra only

Features of a typical rib:

Head: articulates with demifacets or full facets of thoracic
vertebral bodies
Neck: curved region connecting head and tubercle
Tubercle: articulates with transverse process of thoracic vertebra
Angle: where shaft bends and curves anteriorly, most common site
for fractures
Costal groove: region where intercoastal nerves and blood vessels
run
Costal cartilage: articulates with sternum

Features of atypical 1st rib:
    Flat, shorter , and has a rougher surface compared to other
   ribs
   Head: articulates with full facets on T1
   Scalene tubercle: separates two smooth grooves on the
   superior view of rib
    Anterior to scalene tubercle: groove for subclavien vein
    (superficial groove)
    Posterior to scalene tubercle: groove for subclavien artery (
   deeper groove)


Other Atypical ribs
Typical vs Atypical RIbs

Thoracic Vertebra, Its Features, and Articulation

There are 12 thoracic vertebrae which all articulate with ribs
   Contains a heart shaped body which contains demifacets or
    full facets ( T1, T10T12) for articulation with head of rib
   Spinous process: posterior and inferior process
   Transverse processes: lateral processes which articulate with
   tubercles of ribs; floating ribs do not articulate with transverse
   process
   Lamina: broad and flat overlapping wall which connects
   transverse processes with spinous process
   Superior articular processes: superior projections which
   articulates with inferior articular processes of vertebra above it
    Inferior articular processes: inferior projections which
   articulate with superior articular processes of vertebra below it
   Superior and inferior articulating processes lock with adjacent
   vertebrae to form the Z-joint ( also known as zygapophyseal
    joint or facet joint) allowing for gliding

heart.
Identify the borders of the heart (right, inferior,
left, superior).
Locate the coronary sulcus (atrioventricular
groove) and the anterior and posterior
interventricular sulci.

the heart (superior vena cava, inferior vena
cava, pulmonary trunk, aorta, pulmonary
veins).
Recognize the auricles of the right and left atria.

The 4 chambers, left and right atria and
ventricles

 1. Left and right Coronary (atrioventricular) sulci:
They run around the heart between the atria and the
ventricles.
   Right coronary artery, on the right side.
   Circumflex artery, on the left side.
   Great cardiac vein, on the left side.
   Coronary sinus, on the posterior part, where the
   great cardiac vein drains into it.

2. Anterior interventricular sulcus: It lies on the
sternocostal (anterior) surface, between the two
ventricles.
    Left anterior descending (anterior interventricular)
   artery.
   Great cardiac vein, which begins here and then
   climbs into the coronary sulcus.

3. Posterior interventricular sulcus: It lies on the
diaphragmatic (inferior) surface, between the two
ventricles.
    Posterior interventricular (posterior descending)
   artery. It comes from the right coronary artery in
   most people, which is called right dominance.
   Middle cardiac vein.

Transverse: open at both ends, between the great
arteries in front and the great veins and left atrium
behind.

Oblique: closed at one end, behind the left atrium and
bounded by the pulmonary veins and IVC.

Transverse sinus
      It is a tunnel-shaped passage inside the pericardial
   cavity, running left to right across the base of the
   heart.
    In front: the ascending aorta and the pulmonary
   trunk. Behind: the superior vena cava, and the roof
   of the left atrium. Ends: it is open at both the left and
   right ends.
  Why it exists: in the embryo, the arterial end (aorta
   and pulmonary trunk) and the venous end (vena
   cavae and pulmonary veins) of the heart tube get
   separate reflections of serous pericardium. The gap
   between the two reflections is the transverse sinus.
    Clinical use: surgeons pass a clamp or ligature
   through it to compress the aorta and pulmonary
   trunk together. This controls bleeding and is used
  when starting cardiopulmonary bypass.





Oblique sinus
     It is a blind-ended pouch behind the heart.
    In front the posterior wall of the left atrium.Behind
   the pericardial sac, with the oesophagus lying just
   beyond it. Boundaries  it is bounded by the
   pericardial reflections around the four pulmonary
   veins and the inferior vena cava. Its closed end
   points upward.
      It opens downward and to the left, into the rest of
   the pericardial cavity.

Position and location
   The heart lies in the middle mediastinum, inside the
   pericardial sac, behind the body of the sternum and
   the costal cartilages.
   About two-thirds of it lies to the left of the midline
   and one third to the right.
      It sits on the central tendon of the diaphragm.

It is tilted so that the right side faces forward and the
left side faces backward and to the left.
The base faces posteriorly and to the right, mainly
formed by the left atrium. The apex points
anteriorly, inferiorly and to the left.
Apex location: left 5th intercostal space. The apex
beat is felt here.
Vertebral level: roughly T5 to T8.

Four chambers


Right atrium
   Forms the right border of the heart.
      It receives the superior and inferior venae cavae
   and the coronary sinus.
      It has the right auricle.

Right ventricle
   Forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface.
      It receives blood from the right atrium through the
   tricuspid valve and pumps it to the lungs through the
   pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

 Left atrium
   Forms most of the base (posterior surface) of the
   heart.
     It receives four pulmonary veins and has a left
    auricle.
      It sends blood to the left ventricle through the mitral
   (bicuspid) valve.


 Left ventricle
   Forms the apex, the left border and most of the
   inferior (diaphragmatic) surface.
      It has the thickest wall, about three times that of the
   right ventricle.
      It pumps blood through the aortic valve into the
   aorta.

Borders
    Right border: the right atrium, between the
   superior and inferior venae cavae.
    Inferior border: mainly the right ventricle, with a
   small part of the left ventricle near the apex.

Left border: mainly the left ventricle, with a small
   part of the left auricle at the top.
   Superior border: formed by the two atria and their
    auricles, with the ascending aorta and the
   pulmonary trunk emerging from it.

Surfaces
    Sternocostal (anterior): mostly the right ventricle,
   with part of the right atrium and left ventricle.
   Diaphragmatic (inferior): mostly the left ventricle,
   with a small part of the right ventricle.
   Base (posterior): mostly the left atrium, with a small
   part of the right atrium.
   Pulmonary surfaces (left and right): mainly the left
   ventricle on the left, and the right atrium on the
    right. The outer layer of the pericardial sac. It is
   tough, inelastic fibrous connective tissue, mostly
   collagen. The serous pericardium is the thinner inner
   layer. Its parietal layer is fused to the inside of the
   fibrous pericardium. The sac also holds the heart in
   place and stops it from overfilling suddenly. Because
   the fibrous layer is inelastic, fluid collecting inside
   quickly compresses the heart (cardiac tamponade).

Heart Layers Overview
  •Epicardium (Outer layer): Lines the outside of the
     heart. It faces a lumen filled with serous fluid.
⚬Mesothelium: Outermost layer with very flat nuclei and
          loose connective tissue underneath.
  ⚬Submesothelial Connective Tissue: Contains areolar
        tissue and a large layer of adipose tissue.
    ⚬Coronary Vessels & Nerves: Features coronary
   arteries, coronary veins, and nerves buried in the
        adipose tissue of the submesothelium.
    •Myocardium (Middle muscle layer): The thick
 contractile layer. The left ventricle (LV) myocardium is
                          thicker.
 •Endocardium (Inner layer): Lines the chambers of the
        heart. It faces a lumen filled with blood.
  ⚬Endothelium & Basement Membrane: Inner lining.
⚬Subendothelial Connective Tissue: Contains fibroblasts
                and collagen.
⚬Sub-endocardium / Purkinje Fibers: Contains Purkinje
 fibers under the endothelium with little adipose tissue.

Cardiac Muscle: Longitudinal Section
•Uni- or Binucleated Central Nucleus: Cells feature central nuclei.
        •Branching: Cardiac muscle fibers branch out.
       •Striations: Visible cross-striations along the fibers.
   •Intercalated Discs (ICD): Specialized junctional complexes
                    located between cells.
 •Endomysium Connective Tissue: Composed of fibroblasts and
            collagen surrounding the muscle fibers.
   •Capillaries: Visible endothelium nuclei and red blood cells
                            (RBCs).
